transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came because... oh, it's just so hard to admit out loud. But it's these nights of eating. I end up sitting there in my living room, just surrounded by crumbs and empty containers. 

You know, it's funny, I used to save all those little plastic deli containers for the church bake sales. We used to have them every first Sunday of the month, right after service. My friend Martha would always bring these beautiful lemon bars, though between you and me, she used the boxed mix and tried to pass it off as from scratch. I never said a word, of course, because it's not my place to judge, but everybody in the congregation knew. She'd put a little powdered sugar on top to hide the edges... 

But, oh, I'm sorry, what was I saying? Right, the eating. I sit there in the middle of the night with all that mess around me, and I just feel so... ashamed. So disgusted with myself, honestly. It weighs on me so heavy that I can hardly even bring myself to pray. And the next morning, I can't even look folks at church in the eye. I just feel so terrible about what I've done.

Can you describe what happens during these nighttime eating episodes? Do you feel like you're eating a much larger amount of food than what most people would eat in a similar time period and under similar circumstances?

Well, yes, I suppose it is a lot of food. Much more than a person ought to eat. On a bad night... oh, it's just awful... I can start with a plate of leftover casserole. Usually from a funeral luncheon. You know, I help organize the repasts at St. Jude's, and people are always so generous with their casseroles. Mary Ellen makes this green bean one with those little crispy onions on top, but she always uses too much salt. I've told her, I said, "Mary Ellen, Frank's blood pressure can't take all that sodium," but she just waves me off. She's always been stubborn, even back when we were in high school together. We used to take the bus down to the Woolworth's and... 

Oh, right, the food. Yes, so I'll start with the casserole, and before I even realize what's happening, I've eaten the whole thing. And then I'll move on to half a pan of brownies, some biscuits, and whatever chicken salad is left in the fridge. Just... all in one sitting. It's like I can't stop myself once I start.
When you start eating all that food, do you feel like you can't stop or control what you're doing once you've started?

Well, yes, exactly. Once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside entirely. Even while I'm sitting there telling myself, "Belinda, stop now," my hands just keep reaching for more. I can't seem to make myself stop. 

It reminds me of how my hands used to just work on their own when I was knitting those baby blankets for the hospital. I must have knitted a hundred of them over the years. Pale yellow, mostly, because you never know if it's going to be a boy or a girl, and I always thought yellow was so cheerful. My sister Margaret used to say I was wasting my time, that they probably just threw them out, but Margaret's always had a sour outlook. Ever since her husband left her for that dental hygienist—what was her name, Cindy? Sandy? Something with an S. She had that big hair, you know the kind, sprayed so stiff it wouldn't move in a hurricane. 

But yes, it's just like that. I can't control it. My hands just keep going and going, and I can't stop eating.
Do these nighttime eating episodes cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life in any way?

Oh, it causes me a great deal of distress, doctor. It really does. It's getting to the point where it's affecting my whole life. I've even started turning down some of my bridge nights with the girls. And I've been backing out of my kitchen duties at the church, too. I just... I'm so worried someone is going to notice all the missing leftovers, or they'll look at me and ask why I seem so ashamed all the time. 

It breaks my heart to miss bridge night, though. We've been playing every Thursday for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We rotate houses, you know. Last week was supposed to be at Helen's. Helen always sets out those little mints, the ones in the pastel colors with the little white beads on them? I don't know where she finds them these days. You used to be able to get them at the five-and-dime, but ever since they closed down and put in that cell phone store... well, nothing is the same anymore. The young man who works there, he helped me with my phone once when the screen went all black, but he talked so fast I couldn't understand a word he said. 

But yes, I just can't bring myself to go to bridge or the church kitchen lately. The worry is just too much.
Do these nighttime eating episodes happen after you've already gone to sleep and then wake up, or do you usually eat that way while staying up late, without having slept first?

Well, no, I haven't gone to sleep yet when it happens. I'm usually just staying up late. I've always been a bit of a night owl, truth be told. Ever since Frank—my late husband—worked the second shift at the auto plant. That was back in the eighties, before they downsized and let half the town go. He'd come home around midnight smelling like motor oil and that heavy industrial soap they used in the locker rooms. 

It was a green soap, kind of gritty? We used to buy something similar at the hardware store for the garage, but the hardware store closed down years ago. Mr. Henderson ran it, and his son was supposed to take over, but the son moved to Florida to open a bait shop of all things. Imagine that, leaving a perfectly good hardware business to sell worms and tackle in Florida! He always was a strange boy, though. He used to ride his bicycle right through my flower beds. 

But anyway, I used to stay up waiting for Frank to get home so I could heat up his dinner, and I suppose I just never lost the habit of being awake at that hour. The house gets so quiet, and I'll just be sitting there in my armchair... so yes, I haven't been to bed at all when the eating starts. I'm just up.

Doctor: When you're eating all that food at night, would you say you're fully awake and aware of what you're doing, or do you feel like you're in a kind of daze or not completely in control of yourself?

Well, I'm certainly awake. I know I'm sitting there at the kitchen island, and I know exactly what I'm putting in my mouth, even if I can't seem to stop myself. It's not like I'm sleepwalking or anything like that. 

My cousin Betty used to sleepwalk. Oh, it was the strangest thing. She'd get up in the middle of the night and start rearranging the furniture in her living room. Her husband would wake up and find the sofa pushed all the way against the television set, and Betty fast asleep on the rug. They finally had to put a little bell on their bedroom door so he'd hear her leaving. It was one of those brass bells you see on shop doors, you know? She bought it at an antique store in Vermont when they went to see the leaves change. I've always wanted to go to Vermont in the fall. I hear the colors are just magnificent, all those reds and golds. We only get brown leaves here, mostly. They just dry up and fall off the oak trees in the backyard, and then I have to pay the neighbor's boy to rake them up. He charges twice what his brother used to charge, but what can you do? 

But no, I'm definitely awake. I'm just sitting there, fully awake, watching myself eat everything in sight.

latest_inference.note: The patient confirmed that they are fully awake during the nighttime eating episodes, which rules out any parasomnia-related conditions like sleep-related eating disorder (F51.5). The continued presence of loss of control over eating, distress, and absence of compensatory behaviors supports Night Eating Syndrome (F50.81) as the most accurate diagnosis. No features of depression (F32.9) or anxiety (F43.22) are prominently present beyond the distress related to the eating behavior itself.
